(b) Explain why a merge can propagate up the tree. (c) Explain the single case in which a merge decreases the tree's height, and why that keeps all leaves at the same depth.
52.5 core Lazy deletion. (a) Why do most engines defer the merge instead of rebalancing on every delete — what does an eager merge lock? (b) Define index bloat and describe how occupancy and range-scan cost change after a large delete under lazy deletion. (c) Name the operation that reclaims the space and explain why it produces a denser tree than the deletes left behind.
52.6 core Occupancy arithmetic. (a) State the average occupancy random insertion produces and the size ratio 1/ln 2 it implies. (b) A table's data would fit in 1,000,000 densely-packed index pages; estimate the page count of the same index built by random row-by-row insertion. (c) Explain two distinct costs that the extra pages impose (think buffer pool and height).
52.7 cost Latch coupling cost. (a) For a read descending a height-4 B-tree with crabbing, how many latches are held at any one moment, and why is that enough? (b) For a naive insert that must guard against a split, how many latches might it hold on the path, and what determines when it can release the ancestors? (c) Explain in cost terms why near-full nodes make the naive insert scheme collapse toward serial execution.
52.8 faded Worked, with the last step for you. A search and a concurrent insert touch the same leaf; the search released the parent latch just before the insert split that leaf.
Step 1 (given): the insert splits the leaf, moving the upper half of its keys — including the search's target — to a new right sibling.
Step 2 (given): the search is now holding a leaf that no longer contains its key.
Step 3 (given): in a plain B-tree the search would wrongly report the key absent (the split race).
Step 4 (you): Explain what the Blink-tree's right-link and high key let the search do instead, and why that means the search never needed to hold the parent latch.
52.9 mixed For each, name the mechanism responsible — borrow, merge, lazy deletion, bulk-loading, or the right-link — and why: (a) an index stays large on disk after most rows are deleted; (b) a rebuilt index is ~30% smaller than the one it replaced; (c) an under-full node is fixed with a single key movement and no structural change; (d) the tree's height decreases; (e) a search recovers from a concurrent split by moving sideways.
52.10 mixed Classify each as true or false and fix the false ones: (a) “A B-tree's height can decrease only when a merge empties the root.” (b) “Random insertion fills B-tree nodes to about 85% on average.” (c) “Bulk-loading is denser than insertion because it never splits.” (d) “Deleting rows automatically shrinks the index on disk.” (e) “With the Blink-tree right-link, a descending search must hold a latch on the parent to be safe against a split.”
52.11 stretch Symmetry and its limits. (a) Argue that insert-with-split and delete-with-merge are exact mirrors, matching each step of one to a step of the other. (b) Given that symmetry, explain why real systems implement the split faithfully but usually defer the merge — what breaks the symmetry in practice. (c) Explain how deferring the merge, plus the ln 2 occupancy of insertion, together mean a long-lived B-tree drifts toward lower density over time, and what operational practice counters the drift.
52.12 lab On your own machine (any language): (a) Implement a working B-tree of minimum degree t with insert (split) and delete (borrow and merge). (b) Insert keys in a seeded random order and measure the average node occupancy for a few values of t; confirm it approaches ln 2 ≈ 0.693. (c) Then delete most of the keys and report that the height shrinks and every surviving key is still found. (d) State your toolchain and explain why occupancy and height are structural outcomes of the operation sequence, not wall-clock timings.

Chapter 53 — The Log-Structured Merge-Tree: Trading Reads for Writes

Before you start: Chapter 46 (the device measurement that rules everything here: sequential streaming ~916 MB/s versus random 4 KiB access ~19 MB/s, ~49× slower — the gap the LSM-tree exploits), Chapter 41 (durability: an fsync'd append to a log is what makes an in-memory write survive a crash), Chapter 47 (pages and the on-disk file), Chapter 49 (the sequential append a heap file already showed is cheap), Chapter 51 and Chapter 52 (the B-tree — the read-optimized, update-in-place engine this one is the mirror of).  ·  The B-tree finds the page a key belongs on and updates it there, in place, which makes every write a random page update. This chapter builds the engine that refuses to do that: it never updates in place, buffers writes in memory, and flushes them as sorted, immutable files — turning random writes into sequential ones, and paying the bill at read time instead.

Before you read on

From memory: (1) Chapter 46 — on this machine sequential streaming ran at ~916 MB/s and random 4 KiB access at ~19 MB/s; about how many times slower is random, and why does that gap exist on both flash and disk? (2) Chapter 52 — a B-tree write updates the page where the key belongs; what does that make each write, in device terms? (3) Predict: suppose you make every write cheap by never seeking — just append each new key-value to the end of a file, in arrival order. Writes are now pure sequential appends. What have you made catastrophically expensive, and for which operation? Write your guess; §53.1 and §53.3 answer it.

The B-tree of the last two chapters is the read-optimized storage engine: it keeps keys sorted in a shallow tree of pages so any key is found in a handful of fetches, and it maintains that order by updating pages in place — finding the leaf a key belongs on and writing it there. That in-place discipline is exactly what makes reads and range scans excellent, and exactly what makes every write a random page update, paying the Chapter 46 random-access cost — ~49× slower than sequential on the very machine we measured. For a write-heavy workload — a metrics firehose, an event log, a high-ingest key-value store — that random-write tax dominates, and no amount of B-tree tuning removes it, because it is inherent in keeping the data sorted on disk as it arrives. The log-structured merge-tree (LSM-tree), introduced by O'Neil, Cheng, Gawlick, and O'Neil in 1996 and made ubiquitous by Google's Bigtable and its descendants (LevelDB, RocksDB, Cassandra, HBase), takes the opposite bet: it never updates in place. Writes go into a sorted in-memory structure and are periodically flushed to disk as whole, immutable, sorted files written sequentially; reads consult memory first and then those files, newest to oldest; and the files are merged in the background to keep their number down. The trade is deliberate and total — the LSM-tree makes writes sequential and cheap and pays for it at read time and in space — and it is the write-optimized counterpart to the read-optimized B-tree. This chapter builds it in five steps: the inversion, and why appending is not enough by itself (§53.1); the write path — the memtable, the write-ahead log that makes it durable, and the flush to an immutable SSTable (§53.2); the read path — check memory, then the sorted files newest to oldest, with a tombstone for deletes, reproduced in a working model (§53.3); the resulting read amplification and space cost that pile up as files accumulate, and its named trap (§53.4); and what all of this hands to the compaction chapter that follows (§53.5).

On the code in this chapter. One Python program (CPython 3.10.12 on this machine's Intel Core i7-12700H) implementing a faithful LSM write and read path: writes land in a sorted in-memory memtable; when it reaches a flush threshold it is written, in sorted order, as an immutable SSTable and a fresh memtable begins; a read checks the memtable and then the SSTables newest to oldest, stopping at the first hit; and a delete writes a tombstone. The program reports two structural quantities — how many SSTables accumulate, and how many of them a point read must scan (its read amplification) — and confirms that the newest write wins and a tombstone shadows older values. These are counts determined by the code's logic and a seeded key stream, not wall-clock timings. Where a sequential-versus-random write cost appears, it is the Chapter 46 device figures (~916 MB/s sequential, ~19 MB/s random) measured earlier in this volume and cited here, not re-measured (a hardware-counter profiler, perf, is not installed on this machine).

53.1 The inversion: make writes sequential, pay at read time

Start from the cost that defines the problem. On the machine of Chapter 46 a large sequential write streams at ~916 MB/s while random 4 KiB access manages ~19 MB/s — a ~49× gap, and it is not an accident of one device: seeks cost on disk, and even flash pays for random writes through its erase-block granularity and garbage collection. A B-tree write is a random write (it updates the leaf a key belongs on), so the B-tree sits on the slow side of that gap for every insert. The obvious escape is to stop seeking: never place a key where it belongs, just append each new key-value to the end of a file in arrival order. Writes are now pure sequential appends at ~916 MB/s — the fast side of the gap. But this naive log has made one thing catastrophic, which is the answer to the opener: a read for a key must now scan the entire log, because the log is in arrival order, not key order, and the key could be anywhere — and if the key was overwritten, the newest value is whichever copy is latest in the log, so you cannot even stop at the first match from the front. An append-only log is the best possible write structure and the worst possible read structure. The LSM-tree is the engineering that keeps the sequential-write win while making reads tractable again, and it does so with one idea: keep the in-memory buffer sorted, and flush it sorted. Then the on-disk files are each internally sorted (so a key is found in one file by binary search, not a scan), and there are few enough of them (because each flush is a whole batch, not one key) that a read consults a manageable handful. The LSM-tree is not “a log” in the naive sense; it is a log of sorted runs, and that word “sorted” is what turns an unreadable append log into a real index. What it cannot escape is that reads now touch several sorted files instead of one tree — the bill the write side deferred — and the rest of the chapter is about paying it.

Quick check

Appending every write to a log in arrival order makes writes maximally cheap. Which operation does it make catastrophically expensive, and why? What single property must the buffer and its flushed files have to make that operation tractable again? (Answer after the next section.)

53.2 The write path: the memtable, the WAL, and the immutable SSTable

A write enters the LSM-tree at the memtable: an in-memory, sorted, mutable structure — typically a balanced tree or a skip list, so inserts stay ordered and cheap — that accumulates recent writes. Because the memtable is in volatile memory, a crash would lose it, so every write is first appended to a write-ahead log (WAL) on disk (Chapter 41) — a sequential, fsync'd append, itself cheap — so that after a crash the memtable can be reconstructed by replaying the log. This is the crucial detail that makes the LSM-tree durable without a random write: the only synchronous disk write on the insert path is a sequential append to the WAL; the sorted placement happens in memory. When the memtable grows past a threshold, it is flushed: its contents, already sorted, are written out in one sequential pass as an immutable on-disk file — historically called an SSTable (Sorted String Table, the name from Bigtable) — and once the SSTable is safely on disk the corresponding WAL segment can be discarded and a fresh empty memtable takes over. Two properties of that flushed file are load-bearing for everything after. It is sorted, so a lookup within one SSTable is a binary search, not a scan, and two SSTables can be merged by a linear merge like the merge step of mergesort. And it is immutable: once written, an SSTable is never modified in place — not to update a key, not to delete one — which is what keeps writes sequential (no random rewrites ever happen) and also makes the files trivially safe to read concurrently and to cache, since nothing mutates underneath a reader. An update to an existing key does not find and change it; it simply writes the new value into the memtable, which will flush to a newer SSTable, and the newer value shadows the old one at read time. The disk fills with a stack of immutable sorted files, newest on top, and no random write was ever issued.

The same idea three ways: buffer in memory and flush sorted, turning random writes into sequential ones

1. In words. Instead of updating the page a key belongs on (a random write), the LSM-tree collects writes in a sorted in-memory memtable and flushes the whole batch as one immutable sorted file in a single sequential pass. Every disk write it issues is sequential; the price is that a key's current value may live in memory or in any of the flushed files.

2. As a picture. Figure 53.1: writes flow into a memtable box; an arrow labeled “flush (sequential)” drops a sorted SSTable onto a growing stack of immutable files below, newest on top; a WAL append sits beside the memtable guarding durability.

3. As numbers. The write the LSM-tree avoids is the ~19 MB/s random 4 KiB update of Chapter 46; the writes it issues — the WAL append and the flush — are the ~916 MB/s sequential stream, the same ~49× faster side of the gap. The cost moves to reads and space, quantified in §53.3–§53.4.

(Answer to the §53.1 quick check: a naive arrival-order append log makes reads catastrophic — a lookup must scan the whole log, since the key could be anywhere and the newest copy is wherever it was last written. The property that makes reads tractable is sortedness: keep the memtable sorted and flush it sorted, so each on-disk file is internally sorted — found by binary search, mergeable linearly — and a read consults a handful of sorted runs instead of scanning an unordered log.)

53.3 The read path: newest wins, tombstones, and read amplification

Because a key's value can live in the memtable or in any flushed SSTable, and because a newer write shadows an older one, a read must consult the sources newest first and stop at the first hit. It checks the memtable; then, if not found, the SSTables from newest to oldest; the first source that contains the key holds its current value, and the search stops — anything older is a superseded version and must not be returned. This ordering is also how deletion works, and the mechanism is worth stating plainly because it surprises people: since SSTables are immutable, a delete cannot go back and erase the key from the older files where it still sits. Instead a delete writes a tombstone — a marker “this key is deleted” — into the memtable, which flushes to a newer SSTable like any other write. A later read finds the tombstone first (it is the newest entry for that key), stops, and reports the key absent, even though older SSTables still physically contain the old value. A delete, in an LSM-tree, is a write. The working model reproduces the whole path — newest-wins reads, tombstone-shadows-value deletes, and the count of files a read must touch:

LSM write path (100000 writes, keys drawn from a 40k-key space so keys are overwritten):
  flush_threshold=1000: 100000 writes -> 99 SSTables on disk
     avg SSTables scanned per point read: hit=35.9   miss=99  (a miss must touch ALL runs)
  flush_threshold=5000: 100000 writes -> 19 SSTables on disk
     avg SSTables scanned per point read: hit= 7.6   miss=19  (a miss must touch ALL runs)

correctness: newest write wins; a tombstone shadows an older value
  put v1, put v2, flush;  put v3, flush   -> get = v3           (newest of two SSTables)
  delete, flush                           -> get = None         (tombstone shadows v2,v3, which still sit on disk)
  SSTables on disk: 3  (the dead values are NOT reclaimed until compaction)

Two facts jump out. First, the model is correct: the newest write wins, and a tombstone hides values that physically still exist in older files — deletion by shadowing, not erasure. Second, and this is the whole cost of the design: a point read may have to scan many SSTables. A lookup for a key that is absent is the worst case — it finds the key in none of them, so it must touch every run before concluding “not here” (99 files at the small flush threshold, 19 at the larger). This is read amplification: the LSM-tree turned one logical read into many physical file probes, the exact mirror of the write amplification a B-tree pays. The flush threshold trades one against the other — a larger memtable means fewer, bigger SSTables (less read amplification) but more memory held and more lost on a crash before the WAL is replayed. And notice the deletion line: after deleting the key, three SSTables still sit on disk, two of them holding now-dead values plus a tombstone. The LSM-tree's write path has quietly created three problems that only grow with time — too many files to read, dead values wasting space, and tombstones that must be carried until every older copy they shadow is gone — and none of them is fixed by anything on the write path. Fixing them is the job of compaction, the next chapter; this chapter's job is to make you feel why compaction is not optional.

Quick check

Why must a read consult its sources newest-first and stop at the first hit — what would returning an older copy get wrong? And why is a point miss, not a hit, the worst case for read amplification? (Answer after the communicate box.)

Trap: a delete is a write — the tombstone, and the range-scan-over-tombstones cliff

The intuition “deleting frees space and speeds things up” is exactly backwards in an LSM-tree, and it bites hard. A delete does not remove anything: it writes a tombstone, which adds data, consumes a memtable slot and eventually an SSTable entry, and leaves the old value physically on disk in older files until a later compaction finally drops both. So deleting a million keys makes the store temporarily larger, not smaller. Worse is the range scan. A range scan over an LSM-tree must merge the runs across the whole key range and skip past every tombstone in it, because a tombstone might be shadowing a live value in an older run and the scan cannot know without reading it. A key range that has been heavily deleted — say a queue table where rows are inserted and soon deleted, or a time range that was bulk-purged — can therefore hold thousands of tombstones with almost no live rows, and a scan of it reads all of them to return almost nothing: a query that touches “ten live rows” can physically read tens of thousands of tombstones and stall. This is a real and famous operational cliff (Cassandra operators know it as the “tombstone scan” problem, complete with warning thresholds). “It's just a few deleted rows, the query should be fast” and “deletes clean up after themselves” are both false on an LSM-tree: deletes are writes that linger, and reads pay for them until compaction removes them. The honest mental model is that in an LSM-tree every operation, including delete, is an append, and space and read cost are reclaimed only by the background merge — never by the delete itself.

Say it like a systems engineer

Try it first. A teammate says: “We moved our high-ingest service from Postgres to an LSM key-value store and writes got dramatically faster — great. But now point reads are noticeably slower than before, and the data directory is almost twice the size of the actual data. Did we misconfigure something?” Cover the paragraph and answer in four or five sentences, drawing on §53.1–§53.4.

Model answer. “Nothing is misconfigured — you're seeing the LSM-tree's trade working exactly as designed. It made writes fast by never updating in place: writes buffer in memory and flush as immutable sorted files, so every disk write is sequential instead of a random page update. The bill for that lands on reads and space. A point read has to check the memtable and then the sorted files newest-to-oldest, so it probes several files instead of one B-tree — that's read amplification, and it's why reads got slower. And the near-2× size is space amplification: old versions of updated keys and tombstones for deleted keys physically stay in older files until a background compaction merges the files and drops the dead entries. So it's the write-optimized side of a deliberate trade, not a bug. What you tune is compaction — how aggressively the files are merged — which buys back read speed and space at the cost of extra background write work; that's the knob, and it's the subject of the next chapter.” Naming the in-place-vs-append inversion, read amplification, space amplification, and compaction as the knob is the senior register.

53.4 Why the files must be merged: read amplification and space, over time

The write path of §53.2 has one relentless consequence: SSTables only accumulate. Every flush adds a file and none is ever removed by writing, so a long-running LSM-tree drifts toward a large stack of sorted runs, and the read path of §53.3 pays for every one of them. Read amplification grows with the file count — a point miss touches all of them, and even a hit touches every file newer than the one holding the key. Space grows too, and for two distinct reasons the write path guarantees: obsolete versions, because updating a key writes a new copy while the old copy sits in an older file unremoved, so a hot key that is updated a thousand times has a thousand versions on disk with only the newest live; and tombstones, because a delete adds a marker and cannot remove the shadowed value, so deleted data occupies space until every copy it shadows is gone. Left alone, an LSM-tree becomes slower to read and larger on disk without bound, even as its logical contents stay the same size. The structure therefore has a mandatory second half that the write path implies but does not perform: compaction, a background process that reads several SSTables, merges their sorted contents into fewer (or one) new sorted SSTables, and along the way keeps only the newest version of each key and drops tombstones whose shadowed values it has now also seen and discarded. Compaction is what bounds the file count (bounding read amplification), reclaims the space of dead versions and tombstones (bounding space amplification), and it is the reason the “LSM” has “merge” in its name. It is not free — it re-reads and re-writes data that was already written, which is write amplification, the LSM's own version of the B-tree's random-write cost, only deferred and sequential — and how aggressively to run it is the central tuning decision, trading read amplification and space against write amplification. That three-way trade — the amount of extra reading, extra writing, and extra space you accept — is the subject of the next chapter, and it is why there is no single “best” LSM configuration: you choose which of the three to spend.

(Answer to the §53.3 quick check: a read must go newest-first and stop at the first hit because a newer write shadows an older one — the first source containing the key holds its current value, and any older copy is a superseded version that would be wrong to return. A point miss is the worst case because the key is in no source, so the read can never stop early: it must probe the memtable and every SSTable before it can conclude the key is absent — the full read amplification, every time.)

53.5 What to carry forward

The LSM-tree is the write-optimized storage engine, the mirror of the read-optimized B-tree. It exploits the Chapter 46 fact that sequential access is ~49× faster than random by never updating in place: writes go to a sorted in-memory memtable, made durable by a sequential WAL append, and are flushed in one sequential pass as an immutable, sorted SSTable — so every disk write is sequential and no random page update is ever issued (§53.1–§53.2). Reads pay for that: a lookup checks the memtable, then the SSTables newest to oldest, stopping at the first hit; a delete is a write of a tombstone that shadows older values rather than erasing them; and a point miss must touch every file — read amplification, reproduced at 19–99 files scanned in the working model (§53.3). Because files only accumulate and dead versions and tombstones only pile up, the structure requires compaction to merge runs, drop obsolete versions and tombstones, and bound both read amplification and space — at the cost of write amplification (§53.4).

Step back and the two engines of this part are now both on the table, and they are exact opposites built on the same storage manager. The B-tree keeps data sorted on disk and updates it in place: reads and range scans are excellent (one shallow tree, one path), writes are random and expensive, and space is tight (~69% full). The LSM-tree keeps data sorted in memory and appends it to disk in immutable runs: writes are sequential and cheap, reads and range scans pay to merge many runs, and space is loose (dead versions and tombstones linger until compaction). Neither is better; they sit at opposite ends of a trade between the cost of reading, the cost of writing, and the cost of storage — and the next chapter makes that trade precise, showing how compaction strategy lets an LSM-tree slide along it, and why you cannot minimize all three at once. The chapter after builds the read-side rescue the LSM-tree needs — the Bloom filter that lets a point read skip files that cannot contain the key, cutting the read amplification §53.3 measured. And the final chapter of the part puts B-tree and LSM-tree side by side and answers the question the whole part has been building toward: given a workload, which engine, and why. The B-tree gave you fast selective reads; the LSM-tree gives you fast durable writes; the art is knowing which bill you would rather pay.

Can you… without looking?
  • State the inversion: what the LSM-tree refuses to do, and which device fact of Chapter 46 makes that pay.
  • Explain why a naive arrival-order append log is unreadable, and what property fixes it.
  • Trace the write path: memtable, WAL, flush to an immutable SSTable, and why each disk write is sequential.
  • Trace a read: which sources, in what order, and why newest wins; and explain how a tombstone deletes.
  • Define read amplification and space amplification, and say why both grow over time without intervention.
  • Explain why compaction is mandatory and what it costs (write amplification).

(b) Explain precisely why a point read on that log is catastrophic, including why you cannot stop at the first match found scanning from the front. (c) State the single property that turns the unreadable log into a real index, and how it helps both a single-file lookup and a two-file merge.
53.5 core The read path. (a) List the sources a read consults and the order, and explain why newest must win. (b) Trace the model's sequence — put v2 (flush), put v3 (flush), delete (flush) — and give the result of a read after each flush, naming what shadows what. (c) Explain why a point miss is the worst case for read amplification.
53.6 core Immutability. (a) Give two distinct things the “SSTables are never modified in place” rule buys (think writes, and think concurrent readers). (b) Given immutability, explain how an update to an existing key takes effect at all. (c) Explain how immutability forces deletion to use a tombstone rather than an in-place erase.
53.7 cost Read amplification versus the flush threshold. (a) In the model, 100,000 writes produced 99 SSTables at a 1,000-key flush threshold and 19 at 5,000; explain the relationship. (b) A point miss scans how many files in each case, and why the miss and not the hit is the worst case? (c) What does raising the flush threshold cost, given the memtable is volatile and backed only by the WAL?
53.8 faded Worked, with the last step for you. A queue table inserts rows and deletes each soon after it is processed; a monitoring query scans the table's key range expecting ~10 live rows and times out.
Step 1 (given): each delete writes a tombstone, not an erase, so processed rows leave tombstones behind.
Step 2 (given): the tombstones stay on disk until a compaction removes them and the values they shadow.
Step 3 (given): a range scan must read and skip past every tombstone in the range, because each might shadow a live value in an older run.
Step 4 (you): Explain why a scan expecting ~10 live rows can physically read tens of thousands of entries, and name what must happen for the scan to get fast again.
53.9 mixed For each, name the LSM concept responsible — the memtable, the WAL, SSTable immutability, the tombstone, or read amplification — and why: (a) a crash loses no acknowledged write even though the memtable is in RAM; (b) a point miss must touch every file; (c) a deleted key still occupies disk space; (d) recent writes are served without touching disk at all; (e) an old SSTable can be read concurrently with no locking.
53.10 mixed Classify each as true or false and fix the false ones: (a) “An LSM-tree issues random writes only when the memtable is full.” (b) “A delete in an LSM-tree immediately frees the deleted key's space.” (c) “A read returns the value from the oldest SSTable that contains the key.” (d) “Every disk write an LSM-tree issues — WAL append and flush — is sequential.” (e) “Read amplification means one logical read may become many physical file probes.”
53.11 stretch The mirror. (a) Lay out the B-tree and LSM-tree as opposites on three axes — write cost, read cost, and space — citing the mechanism behind each (in-place update vs append; one tree vs many runs; ~69% fill vs lingering dead versions). (b) Argue that the LSM-tree's write amplification (from compaction) is the counterpart to the B-tree's random-write cost, and why one is deferred and sequential while the other is immediate and random. (c) From the three axes, state the kind of workload for which each engine is the right default.
53.12 lab On your own machine (any language): (a) Implement a memtable (a sorted map) that flushes to an immutable sorted SSTable at a threshold, a read that checks the memtable then SSTables newest-to-oldest, and a delete that writes a tombstone. (b) Drive it with a seeded stream of writes over a small key space and report how many SSTables accumulate and how many a point miss must scan. (c) Verify that the newest write wins and a tombstone hides an older value. (d) State your toolchain and explain why the file count and scan count are structural outcomes of the logic and the key stream, not wall-clock timings.

Chapter 54 — Compaction and Amplification: Tuning the LSM-Tree

Before you start: Chapter 46 (sequential ~916 MB/s vs random ~19 MB/s — compaction is large sequential work, which is why it is affordable at all), Chapter 48 (compaction competes with foreground work for the buffer pool and the device), Chapter 51 and Chapter 52 (the B-tree, whose read cost and ~69% space this chapter's trade is measured against), Chapter 53 (the LSM write and read path this chapter completes — the memtable, the immutable SSTable, tombstones, and the read amplification that made compaction mandatory).  ·  Chapter 53 left the LSM-tree with a growing stack of immutable files, dead versions and tombstones piling up, and reads paying for all of it. This chapter is the missing second half: compaction, the background merge that bounds the mess — and the three amplifications it trades among, the tuning decision at the heart of every LSM store.

Before you read on

From memory: (1) Chapter 53 — why do SSTables only accumulate, and what two kinds of dead data pile up in them over time? (2) Chapter 53 — a point-read miss must touch how many of the files, and what is that cost called? (3) Predict: compaction merges files to cut read amplification and reclaim space — but it does so by re-reading and re-writing data already on disk. So it lowers two costs and raises a third. Name the three costs an LSM-tree trades among, and guess whether any single compaction strategy can make all three small at once. Write your guess; §54.2–§54.3 answer it.

Chapter 53 built the LSM-tree's write and read paths and ended at an uncomfortable place: the write path only ever adds immutable SSTables, so their number grows without bound, dead versions of updated keys and tombstones of deleted ones accumulate, and the read path pays for every file — read amplification and space that climb forever if nothing intervenes. Compaction is what intervenes. It is a background process that takes several SSTables, merges their sorted contents into fewer new SSTables, and along the way keeps only the newest version of each key and drops tombstones once it has passed the values they shadow — bounding the file count (and thus read amplification) and reclaiming the space of dead data. But compaction is not free: it re-reads and re-writes data that was already written, which is write amplification, the LSM-tree's own cost of keeping order, deferred and sequential where the B-tree's was immediate and random. So an LSM-tree is defined by a three-way tension — how much extra reading, extra writing, and extra space it accepts — and the compaction strategy is how you pick your point in that space. This chapter makes the trade precise: what compaction actually does, merging runs and dropping dead data, reproduced on real runs (§54.1); the three amplifications — write, read, space — and the impossibility, the RUM tension, that you cannot minimize all three (§54.2); the two great compaction families, leveled and size-tiered, and an arithmetic model of where each sits on the three axes (§54.3); the tuning that follows and its named trap, that compaction is not free background work but a source of write stalls and device wear (§54.4); and what this completes about the two storage-engine families (§54.5).

On the code in this chapter. One Python program (CPython 3.10.12 on this machine's Intel Core i7-12700H) in two parts. First it runs a concrete compaction: given a set of overlapping sorted runs with updates and tombstones, it merges them keeping the newest value per key and dropping tombstones, and reports how many entries and runs remain — a structural result of the merge logic, showing read amplification and dead space collapse. Second it computes an amplification model: closed-form arithmetic for the write, read, and space amplification of leveled versus size-tiered compaction as a function of the size ratio between levels — exact functions of the parameters, hardware-independent, of the same kind as Chapter 51's fanout arithmetic, and clearly a model of the structure rather than a measurement of any device. Where a sequential-write cost appears it is the Chapter 46 figure cited, not re-measured (a hardware-counter profiler, perf, is not installed on this machine); the amplification numbers are analytical, and labeled as such.

54.1 Compaction: merging runs, dropping dead versions and tombstones

Compaction is a k-way merge of sorted runs, and it is cheap for the same reason the flush was: the inputs are already sorted, so merging them is one linear pass (the merge step of mergesort), reading sequentially and writing sequentially — the ~916 MB/s side of Chapter 46, never a random access. As it merges, compaction does the garbage collection the immutable write path could not. When several runs contain the same key, it keeps only the newest version and discards the rest — reclaiming the space of every superseded update. And when it meets a tombstone, it drops the tombstone and the older values it shadows, since after the merge there is no older run left for those values to hide in — reclaiming deleted data and, finally, the tombstone itself. The output is fewer, larger sorted runs holding only live data, so a subsequent read touches fewer files (lower read amplification) over less dead space (lower space amplification). The working model compacts twenty overlapping runs full of updates and tombstones:

concrete compaction of 20 SSTable runs (updates + tombstones, keyspace 5000):
  entries across runs before: 25934   (a point miss scans all 20 runs)
  entries after full compaction: 3362 (a point read scans 1 run; dead versions + tombstones dropped)
  space reclaimed: 87.0%   read amplification: 20x -> 1x

The twenty runs held 25,934 entries, but most were dead — superseded updates and tombstones — so merging them to keep only the newest live value per key left 3,362 entries in one run: 87% of the physical data was garbage that compaction reclaimed, and read amplification for the compacted range fell from twenty files to one. That is the entire value proposition of compaction in one measurement — it converts the write path's accumulated slack back into a compact, cheap-to-read form. But look at what it cost to get there: to produce the 3,362-entry output, compaction had to read all 25,934 input entries and write 3,362 out, work spent re-processing data that was already on disk. Do this repeatedly, as an LSM-tree must — every byte is rewritten each time its run is compacted into a larger one — and the rewriting adds up to several times the original data volume. That is write amplification, and it is not a flaw to be fixed but the price of order; the only question is how much of it you pay, which depends entirely on how you compact.

Quick check

Compaction merges sorted runs and, doing so, reclaims two kinds of dead data — name them, and say what happens to a tombstone and the value it shadows. Why is the merge itself a cheap (sequential) operation, and what new cost does repeatedly rewriting data create? (Answer in §54.2.)

54.2 The three amplifications, and why you cannot minimize all three

An LSM-tree's behavior is captured by three amplification factors, each a ratio of physical work or space to the logical minimum. Write amplification is the bytes actually written to the device per byte of logical data — greater than one because compaction rewrites data as it merges runs into larger ones. Read amplification is the number of physical accesses per logical read — greater than one because a lookup probes multiple runs. Space amplification is the bytes on disk per byte of live data — greater than one because dead versions and tombstones linger until compaction removes them. Here is the fact that makes LSM tuning an art rather than a lookup: these three are in tension, and lowering one tends to raise another. Compact aggressively — merge runs the moment they appear — and you keep few runs (low read amplification) and little dead data (low space amplification), but you rewrite constantly (high write amplification). Compact lazily — let runs pile up before merging — and you rewrite rarely (low write amplification) but read across many runs (high read amplification) over lots of dead data (high space amplification). You cannot have all three small at once. This is a specific instance of a general law of access-method design, the RUM conjecture of Athanassoulis and colleagues (2016): optimizing any two of read overhead, update overhead, and memory/space overhead comes at the expense of the third. The LSM-tree does not escape the trade the B-tree faced; it relocates it — the B-tree spent its cost as immediate random writes and tight space, the LSM-tree spends its as deferred sequential write amplification and looser space — but the trilemma is the same, and answering the opener's second question: no single compaction strategy makes all three amplifications small. You choose which to spend.

(Answer to the §54.1 quick check: compaction reclaims superseded update versions (keeping only the newest value per key) and deleted data — when it meets a tombstone it drops both the tombstone and the older values it shadowed, since no older run remains to hide them. The merge is cheap because the inputs are sorted, so it is one sequential pass (Chapter 46's fast side), never a random access. The new cost is write amplification: repeatedly rewriting data as it is merged into larger runs writes several times the logical data volume over an item's lifetime.)

54.3 Leveled versus size-tiered compaction: the model

The two dominant compaction strategies sit at opposite ends of the write-versus-read-and-space trade, and both organize SSTables into levels, each level holding runs some size ratio T larger than the one above; the number of levels is L ≈ log-base-T of the data size over the memtable size, so L is small (single digits) for the same logarithmic reason the B-tree is shallow. Leveled compaction keeps exactly one sorted run per level: when a level overflows, its data is merged into the next level's single run, which — because that level is T times bigger — rewrites roughly T bytes for each byte promoted, so write amplification is about T×L; but a read finds at most one run per level (low read amplification) and dead data is squeezed out quickly (low space amplification, near 1). Size-tiered compaction instead lets up to T runs accumulate per level and merges them, all at once, only when a level is full: each byte is written just once per level, so write amplification is only about L; but a read may probe up to T runs at every level (high read amplification, ~T×L) and a full level's worth of dead data can linger (space amplification up to ~T). Same structure, two policies, opposite corners. The model computes all three amplifications for a billion-entry store as the size ratio T varies:

amplification model (N=1e9 entries, flush unit B=1e6; W=write, R=read, S=space amp):
  T    levels | LEVELED  (W / R / S)     | SIZE-TIERED (W / R / S)
   2     10   |   20 /  10 / 1.50        |    10 /  20 /  2.0
   4      5   |   20 /   5 / 1.25        |     5 /  20 /  4.0
  10      3   |   30 /   3 / 1.10        |     3 /  30 / 10.0
  20      3   |   60 /   3 / 1.05        |     3 /  60 / 20.0
  -> leveled trades WRITE amp for low READ and SPACE amp; size-tiered does the reverse. Same tree.

Read the table across and the trade is stark and symmetric. At every size ratio, leveled compaction's read and space amplification are low (a handful of runs, space within ~10–50% of the live data) while it pays in write amplification (20–60×); size-tiered's write amplification is low (3–10×) while it pays in read amplification (up to 60×) and space (up to 2–20× the live data). Raising T makes the tree shallower — fewer levels — which cuts one column and inflates the other: leveled's write amplification climbs with T while its read and space fall; size-tiered's read and space climb with T while its write falls. There is no row where all three are small, which is the RUM tension made numeric. This is why real engines expose compaction as a choice: RocksDB defaults to leveled for read-heavy workloads that need tight space, offers size-tiered (universal) compaction for write-heavy ingest that can tolerate read and space blowup, and Cassandra, HBase, and ScyllaDB expose the same knob — because the “right” answer is a property of the workload, not of the structure.

The same idea three ways: leveled and size-tiered are opposite corners of the write/read/space trade

1. In words. Leveled keeps one run per level, so reads and space are tight but every promotion rewrites a full larger level — high write amplification. Size-tiered lets runs pile up and merges in bulk, so each byte is written about once per level — low write amplification — but reads probe many runs over much dead data. You pick the corner your workload can afford.

2. As a picture. Figure 54.1: a triangle with corners labeled read, write, and space; a “leveled” dot pulled toward low-read/low-space (far from write), a “size-tiered” dot pulled toward low-write (far from read and space) — no dot can sit at the center.

3. As numbers. Modeled here at size ratio T=10 over a billion entries: leveled = write 30 / read 3 / space 1.10; size-tiered = write 3 / read 30 / space 10. The write and read columns literally swap, and space swings 1.1× vs 10× — the trilemma, quantified.

Trap: compaction is not free background work — write stalls, write amplification, and device wear

“Compaction runs in the background, so it's free” is the trap, and it fails at three levels. First, throughput: compaction competes with foreground writes and reads for the same device bandwidth and buffer pool (Chapter 48), so a store under heavy ingest can find its reads and writes slowed by the very merging meant to help them — the background work is real work on the same disk. Second, and sharper, write stalls: if the ingest rate exceeds the rate at which compaction can merge, the unmerged runs (RocksDB's level 0, for instance) pile up, read amplification spikes, and the engine must throttle or stall incoming writes to let compaction catch up — the LSM-tree's “fast writes” turn into periodic write stalls exactly when the write load is highest, which is a classic production surprise. Third, device wear: write amplification means the SSD physically writes several times the logical data — a leveled store at write amplification 30 writes thirty bytes per logical byte — which multiplies flash wear and can dominate the storage budget. The two counter-traps are equal and opposite: switching to size-tiered to cut write amplification (and stalls and wear) can multiply read amplification and double or 10× the space; switching to leveled for read speed and tight space can triple or sextuple the write amplification and its stalls and wear. “Compaction is free” and “just pick the cheap-write policy” are both false: compaction is foreground-affecting work you provision for, and every policy spends one amplification to save another. The honest posture is to measure the workload's read/write/space mix, choose the compaction family that spends the amplification you can most afford, and provision compaction throughput so it keeps up with ingest.

Say it like a systems engineer

Try it first. A teammate proposes: “Our LSM stores are wearing out SSDs and I've read that size-tiered compaction has much lower write amplification. Let's switch every table to size-tiered to cut the writes and save the flash.” Cover the paragraph and answer in four or five sentences, drawing on §54.2–§54.3.

Model answer. “Size-tiered really does cut write amplification — at size ratio 10 it's about 3× versus leveled's ~30×, so the flash-wear worry is legitimate for write-heavy tables. But it isn't free: size-tiered raises the other two amplifications by roughly the same factor it saves. Read amplification can jump to ~30× because a lookup probes many runs per level, and space amplification can hit ~10× because a level's worth of dead versions and tombstones lingers before the bulk merge — so our read-heavy tables would get slower and our disk usage could balloon. The right move is per-table, not global: keep leveled where reads and tight space matter, use size-tiered only on the write-heavy ingest tables that can tolerate the read and space cost, and either way provision enough compaction throughput that we don't hit write stalls under peak ingest. It's a three-way trade — read, write, space — and we should spend the amplification each table can most afford, not minimize writes everywhere.” Naming the RUM trade, the specific read/space cost of size-tiered, and the per-workload choice is the senior register.

54.4 Tuning: choosing which amplification to spend

Everything above resolves into a single design decision made per store, sometimes per table: which amplification can this workload most afford to spend? A read-heavy or space-constrained workload — an index served under tight latency, a store on expensive fast storage — wants leveled compaction, accepting high write amplification to keep reads and space tight. A write-heavy ingest workload — a metrics or event firehose, a log store — wants size-tiered, accepting read and space blowup to keep write amplification and device wear low. The size ratio T is the finer knob within each: larger T means fewer levels, which for leveled raises write amplification while lowering read and space, and for size-tiered does the reverse — so T slides you along the same trade the family already chose. And whatever the choice, compaction throughput must be provisioned to keep pace with ingest, or the write stalls of the trap appear regardless of family. There is no universally correct setting because there is no workload-independent point in a three-way trade; the competent move is to characterize the workload's read/write/space sensitivity and pick the corner accordingly, which is exactly why every production LSM engine ships the choice as configuration rather than baking one in. The tuning is not a defect of the LSM-tree; it is the LSM-tree honestly exposing the trilemma the RUM conjecture says no access method can escape.

Quick check

Leveled and size-tiered compaction each minimize one amplification and pay in the other two — state, for each, which one it minimizes and which two it pays. What does raising the size ratio T do to a leveled store's three amplifications? (Answer below.)

54.5 What to carry forward

Compaction is the background k-way merge that completes the LSM-tree: it merges sorted runs in one sequential pass, keeping only the newest version of each key and dropping tombstones with the values they shadow, which bounds read amplification and reclaims space (the model reclaimed 87% dead data and cut read amplification 20×→1×) — at the cost of write amplification from rewriting data as it merges (§54.1). An LSM-tree trades among three amplifications — write (bytes written per logical byte), read (accesses per logical read), and space (bytes stored per live byte) — and the RUM tension (Athanassoulis et al. 2016) says no strategy makes all three small (§54.2). Leveled compaction (one run per level) minimizes read and space at high write amplification ~T×L; size-tiered (many runs per level, bulk-merged) minimizes write at high read ~T×L and space ~T — opposite corners, quantified by the model (§54.3). The choice is per-workload, the size ratio T is the finer knob, and compaction throughput must keep pace with ingest or write stalls and device wear appear — compaction is provisioned work, not free (§54.4).

With this chapter the two storage-engine families are complete and fully drawn. The B-tree keeps data sorted on disk and updates it in place: excellent reads and range scans, random and immediate write cost, tight ~69% space, and a single point on the trade. The LSM-tree keeps data sorted in memory and appends immutable sorted runs, using compaction to bound the accumulation: cheap sequential writes, read and space costs paid through amplification, and — through the compaction strategy — a whole curve of points on the RUM trade you can slide along. That last difference is the deep one: the B-tree offers one balance of read, write, and space, while the LSM-tree offers a tunable family of balances, which is why write-optimized engines dominate high-ingest systems that need to place their cost deliberately. Two threads remain open for the rest of the part. The read amplification this chapter bounds but does not eliminate — a point read still probes several runs — is attacked next by the Bloom filter, a tiny in-memory structure that lets a read skip runs that provably cannot contain the key, cutting the probes toward one. And the whole question the part has been building toward — given a concrete workload, B-tree or LSM-tree, and at what settings — is answered in the part's final chapter, now that both engines and the amplification vocabulary to compare them are in hand. The B-tree optimizes reads; the LSM-tree optimizes writes and hands you the dial; and knowing which cost your workload can afford to spend is the whole of storage-engine judgment.

Can you… without looking?
  • Describe what compaction does to updates and tombstones, and why the merge itself is cheap.
  • Name the three amplifications and give the one-line reason each exceeds one.
  • State the RUM tension and why no compaction strategy makes all three amplifications small.
  • Contrast leveled and size-tiered compaction on all three axes, with the reason for each.
  • Explain what raising the size ratio T does to a leveled and to a size-tiered store.
  • Explain why compaction is not free — throughput contention, write stalls, and device wear.
Retrieval — closed book

Cover the chapter. Answer from memory; rate confidence first.

  1. R1. What two kinds of dead data does compaction reclaim, and what happens to a tombstone during a merge? (§54.1)
  2. R2. Define write, read, and space amplification, and state the tension among them. (§54.2)
  3. R3. What is the RUM conjecture, and how does it apply to LSM compaction? (§54.2)
  4. R4. Contrast leveled and size-tiered compaction on write, read, and space amplification. (§54.3)
  5. R5. What is a write stall, and how does it arise from treating compaction as free? (§54.4)
Further reading
  • Chen Luo & Michael J. Carey, “LSM-based storage techniques: a survey,” The VLDB Journal 29(1), 2020, pp. 393–418, DOI 10.1007/s00778-019-00555-y. The definitive modern survey: leveled versus tiered compaction and the write/read/space amplification framing this chapter uses. First author Chen Luo; venue, volume, pages, year, and DOI verified via SpringerLink and the ACM Digital Library.
  • Manos Athanassoulis, Michael S. Kester, Lukas M. Maas, Radu Stoica, Stratos Idreos, Anastasia Ailamaki & Mark Callaghan, “Designing Access Methods: The RUM Conjecture,” 19th International Conference on Extending Database Technology (EDBT 2016), pp. 461–466, DOI 10.5441/002/edbt.2016.42. The read/update/memory trilemma of §54.2: optimizing any two overheads costs the third. First author Manos Athanassoulis; venue, year, pages, and DOI verified via the EDBT proceedings and DBLP.
  • Siying Dong, Mark Callaghan, Leonidas Galanis, Dhruba Borthakur, Tony Savor & Michael Strum, “Optimizing Space Amplification in RocksDB,” 8th Biennial Conference on Innovative Data Systems Research (CIDR 2017). A production LSM engine's account of the space/write amplification trade and how leveled compaction and tuning manage it. First author Siying Dong; venue, year, and authorship verified via the CIDR 2017 proceedings (open access, no DOI).
  • Patrick O'Neil, Edward Cheng, Dieter Gawlick & Elizabeth O'Neil, “The Log-Structured Merge-Tree (LSM-Tree),” Acta Informatica 33(4), 1996, pp. 351–385, DOI 10.1007/s002360050048. The original analysis of merging sorted runs across levels and the write-amplification cost that compaction strategy manages. First author Patrick O'Neil; venue, volume, pages, year, and DOI verified via SpringerLink.

Exercises

54.1 warm-up In one sentence, what two kinds of dead data does compaction reclaim, and what does it do with a tombstone it encounters?
54.2 warm-up Name the three amplifications an LSM-tree trades among, and give the one-phrase reason each is greater than one.
54.3 warm-up In one sentence each: which single amplification does leveled compaction minimize, and which does size-tiered minimize?
54.4 core The merge, concretely. (a) The model compacted 20 runs of 25,934 entries down to 3,362; explain in terms of updates and tombstones why so much was dropped. (b) What did read amplification for that range become, and why? (c) Explain why, despite reclaiming 87% of the data, the compaction still wrote — and where that write shows up as an amplification.
54.5 core The RUM tension. (a) State the RUM conjecture in terms of read, update, and memory/space. (b) Explain, using aggressive versus lazy compaction, why lowering read and space amplification raises write amplification. (c) Argue that the B-tree and LSM-tree face the same trilemma and differ only in where they spend it.
54.6 core Leveled versus size-tiered. (a) Describe how each organizes runs within a level (one run vs up to T). (b) From that organization, derive why leveled's write amplification is ~T×L while size-tiered's is ~L. (c) From the same organization, derive why size-tiered's read amplification is ~T×L while leveled's is ~L.
54.7 cost Reading the model. Using the table at size ratio T=10 over a billion entries (leveled 30/3/1.10, size-tiered 3/30/10): (a) which policy would you pick for a read-latency-critical index on expensive storage, and why? (b) which for a metrics firehose on cheap disk, and why? (c) A store writes 1 TB of logical data under leveled compaction at write amplification 30 — roughly how many bytes hit the device, and why does that matter for an SSD?
54.8 faded Worked, with the last step for you. A team runs a high-ingest LSM store with leveled compaction; during traffic spikes, write latency periodically jumps and then recovers.
Step 1 (given): during a spike, incoming writes arrive faster than compaction can merge the newest level's runs.
Step 2 (given): unmerged runs pile up at the top level, and read amplification there climbs.
Step 3 (given): to keep read amplification bounded, the engine throttles incoming writes until compaction catches up.
Step 4 (you): Name this phenomenon, explain why it appears precisely when write load is highest, and give two levers that reduce it (one about provisioning, one about compaction strategy).
54.9 mixed For each, name the responsible concept — write amplification, read amplification, space amplification, leveled compaction, or size-tiered compaction — and why: (a) an SSD wears out faster than the logical write volume suggests; (b) a store's disk usage is 10× its live data; (c) a point read probes many runs at every level; (d) the policy that keeps one run per level; (e) the policy that merges a level's runs only when it fills.
54.10 mixed Classify each as true or false and fix the false ones: (a) “A good compaction strategy makes all three amplifications small.” (b) “Compaction is a random-access operation.” (c) “Size-tiered compaction has lower write amplification but higher read and space amplification than leveled.” (d) “Compaction runs in the background, so it never affects foreground latency.” (e) “Raising the size ratio T lowers the number of levels.”
54.11 stretch The whole trade. (a) Place B-tree, leveled-LSM, and size-tiered-LSM as three points in the read/write/space space, justifying each coordinate. (b) Argue that the LSM-tree offers a curve of points (via T and the compaction family) while the B-tree offers essentially one, and why that flexibility is the LSM-tree's structural advantage for high-ingest systems. (c) Explain why “which engine and which settings” cannot be answered without the workload, tying it to the RUM conjecture.
54.12 lab On your own machine (any language): (a) Implement a k-way merge of several sorted runs that keeps the newest value per key and drops tombstones, and report the input and output entry counts (the reclaimed fraction). (b) Compute, from closed-form arithmetic, the write, read, and space amplification of leveled and size-tiered compaction as functions of the size ratio T and level count L, and tabulate them for a few T. (c) State your toolchain and explain why the reclaimed fraction is a structural outcome of the merge logic and the amplification figures are exact arithmetic of a model — neither a wall-clock timing.

Back Matter

Solutions to Exercises

Worked solutions to the end-of-chapter exercises. Try each before reading its solution.

Chapter 1 — Solutions

1.1 Uniform cost: every basic operation — arithmetic, comparison, and any memory read or write — costs the same fixed unit of time, independent of which address is accessed. The three false assertions about real hardware: (1) all memory accesses cost the same (they vary by orders of magnitude with which tier of the hierarchy holds the data); (2) one instruction takes one unit of time (real CPUs overlap, reorder, and speculate, retiring several per cycle or stalling for hundreds — Chapter 2); (3) operations are independent and equally priced (some ops cost more than others, and a dependent instruction must wait for its input). Method note: the trap is listing symptoms ("caches exist") without naming the underlying assumption they violate — always tie the fact back to uniform cost.
1.2 Fastest to slowest: register (<1 ns) < L1 (~1 ns) < L2 (a few ns) < L3 (~10 ns) < DRAM (~100 ns) < NVMe SSD (tens of µs) < same-datacenter network round trip (hundreds of µs to ~1 ms). All figures are orders of magnitude, machine- dependent (§1.3).
1.3 The memory wall is the large and historically widening gap between how fast a CPU can execute instructions and how long DRAM takes to return a requested byte, because processor throughput improved much faster than DRAM latency for decades (Wulf & McKee, 1995). It makes uniform cost worse over time because the ratio between "one arithmetic op" and "one DRAM access" grew, so pricing a DRAM access at the same "one unit" as an add gets more wrong every hardware generation, not less.
1.4 (a) A few billion ops/second is ~3×109/s, so in 100 ns = 10−7 s the core could do on the order of a few hundred operations (3×109 × 10−7 = 300). (b) A program dominated by random pointer-following spends most of its time waiting for DRAM, leaving the arithmetic units idle for hundreds of potential operations per miss — so it can run at a small fraction of the core's peak throughput even though its big-O looks fine. Order-of-magnitude flags: both the 100 ns and the few-billion-ops/s are approximate and machine-dependent; the point is the ratio (~102), not the exact count. Feed-forward: if this surprised you, revisit §1.2.
1.5 Two explanations: (1) Constant factors dominate at this size. Big-O ignores the constant, and the O(n) bucketing pass may do far more slow memory traffic per element (e.g. scattering writes across buckets spread through DRAM) than the O(n log n) sort, which may stream memory in a cache-friendly order (§1.4). (2) Wrong regime. The asymptotic advantage only shows up once n is large enough; on this dataset n may be small enough that the log n factor is tiny and the bucketing's larger constant wins for the wrong reasons (§1.4). The single settling action: measure both on the real data — big-O cannot answer a "how fast" question. Tempting wrong answer: "the O(n) version must be faster, the benchmark is flawed" — this is trusting the RAM model for a speed question, exactly the §1.4 trap. Feed-forward: §1.4 and the warning box.
1.6 Step 4: The binary search over a small contiguous sorted array is likely to make fewer trips to slow memory per lookup — its handful of accesses are clustered and cache- friendly and the small array may live largely in cache, whereas the hash map's single lookup typically lands on a random heap address and pays a full cache/DRAM miss. So the asymptotically worse structure can win on real hardware because the metric that matters here is costly-memory-accesses per lookup, not operation count. The one thing to do before trusting the argument: benchmark both on the real data and access pattern. Why this final step and not "pick the lower big-O": big-O measures scaling and is silent about the constant factor — where the data lives — which is the entire basis of the argument; only measurement can confirm the memory-access reasoning holds for your actual sizes and hardware. Feed-forward: §1.4; the array-vs-pointer effect is measured in Chapter 3.
1.7 (a) RAM/big-O — the tables grow without bound, so the deciding factor is scaling (quadratic vs linear), which is exactly what big-O captures. (b) Real cost model — same size, same O(n); the 8× gap can only come from constant factors, i.e. memory-access patterns. (c) RAM/big-O — "1000× bigger" is a scaling question. (d) Real cost model — identical length and O(n); the difference is contiguous streaming vs random pointer-chasing through the hierarchy. Method-selection cue: if the question mentions "grows / bigger / scales," reach for big-O; if it fixes the size and asks "why is one faster," reach for the real cost model.
1.8 The claims are not in contradiction. Claim (i) is about the RAM/big-O model (optimal scaling); claim (ii) is about the real cost model (speed at a given size, set by constant factors the memory hierarchy dominates). Both can be true simultaneously: two O(n) algorithms are equally optimal asymptotically yet differ 10× in wall-clock time. To choose for production you still need: the actual input sizes you will run at, and a measurement of both on representative data and hardware. Tempting wrong answer: "'optimal' means fastest, so (i) and (ii) conflict" — conflating asymptotic optimality with speed, the core confusion of §1.4.
1.9 Mechanical sympathy is writing code that works with the grain of the hardware — its memory hierarchy, pipeline, and I/O costs — rather than against it, by understanding enough of how the machine works to get the most from it. The ordering rule: choose a good algorithm first (a bad big-O cannot be rescued by micro-optimization — no cache trick fixes an accidental quadratic), then apply mechanical sympathy to win the constant factor. Failure modes: knowing only big-O → asymptotically optimal code that needlessly runs 10× slow; knowing only micro-optimization → a lovingly hand-tuned O(n2) that dies at scale.
1.10 Three reasons the absolute numbers can't be trusted: (1) they are microarchitecture-specific — cache sizes, latencies, and cycle counts differ across CPU models and generations; (2) they drift with hardware over time, so any printed figure is dated; (3) measured latency depends on context — contention, frequency scaling, what else is resident in cache, and access pattern — so there is no single "the" latency. The ratios are more stable because they reflect the structural reason each tier exists (each is a deliberate size/speed tradeoff a step down from the last), and that layering persists even as every absolute number moves. To get trustworthy numbers: measure on the actual target machine under representative load (a microbenchmark or a profiler), which is the discipline the performance-engineering chapters build. Feed-forward: §1.3; measurement technique in Chapter 3.
1.11 Answers are machine-specific by design; a correct write-up (i) reports real cache-line size (commonly 64 bytes on x86-64) and your actual L1/L2/L3 sizes from getconf/lscpu, (ii) reports two measured per-element times — the in-L1 loop should be markedly faster per element than the exceeds-L3 loop, which is bottlenecked on DRAM bandwidth — and (iii) states the ratio you observed. The learning goal is the habit: on a "how fast" question you generated your own numbers rather than quoting the book's orders of magnitude. Exact values depend entirely on your hardware; the shape (in-cache faster than out-of-cache) is what must appear. Feed-forward: the mechanism behind the ratio is §1.2–1.3 and all of Chapter 3.

Chapter 2 — Solutions

2.1 In order: (1) pipelining — overlap the stages so different instructions occupy different units in the same cycle; (2) superscalar — duplicate execution units and issue several instructions per cycle; (3) out-of-order — reorder execution to run later independent instructions while an earlier one is stalled; (4) speculation / branch prediction — guess a branch's direction and execute down the predicted path so the pipeline need not wait for the branch to resolve.
2.2 Latency is the number of cycles for one instruction to pass through all stages; throughput is how often a new instruction completes. Because the stages overlap — while one instruction is in "execute," the next is in "decode," and so on — a new instruction can finish every cycle even though each individually spends several cycles traversing the pipeline. The two numbers measure different things: time-through-one vs. completions-per-time.
2.3 A data hazard: an instruction needs a result that an earlier, not-yet-finished instruction will produce, so it cannot proceed until that value is ready. A control hazard: the CPU does not yet know which instruction comes next because an unresolved branch determines it. Branch prediction addresses the control hazard — it guesses the branch direction so fetching can continue instead of stalling.
2.4 In loop A each add depends on the previous add's result (they all target one accumulator), forming a single dependency chain: the out-of-order engine can never have more than one add in flight, so the superscalar units sit mostly idle and the loop runs at roughly one add per dependency latency. In loop B the four partial sums are independent, so up to four adds can be in flight at once, keeping multiple execution units busy and finishing in a fraction of the time — same number of additions, more ILP. The enabling condition: floating-point addition is not associative, so B only computes the "same" result if you accept that the grouping (and thus rounding) differs, or the compiler is allowed to reassociate — B's parallelism is possible precisely because its adds have no data dependency between them. Method-selection note: the tell that ILP is the lever is "same operation count, one version serializes them." Feed-forward: §2.3 and the threeways box.
2.5 On P the data-dependent branch resolves in long predictable runs, so the branch predictor is almost always right, speculation is nearly free, and the pipeline stays full. On Q the branch is a patternless coin flip: the predictor is wrong about half the time, and each misprediction flushes the speculatively executed work and refills the pipeline — a penalty on the order of tens of cycles (machine-specific) paid on ~50% of iterations. The extra time on Q is spent flushing and refilling the pipeline, not doing arithmetic. Tempting wrong answer: "Q must be doing more comparisons" — no, the arithmetic is identical; the cost is misprediction, not extra work. Feed-forward: §2.4.
2.6 (a) Average cost per iteration ≈ b + p·k cycles (caveat: k is an order-of-magnitude, microarchitecture-specific figure). (b) The misprediction term dominates when p·k > b, i.e. roughly p > b/k; for a cheap body and a ~tens-of-cycles penalty, even a modest p (a branch that misses a nontrivial fraction of the time) makes misprediction the largest term. (c) Making the branch predictable lowers p (the predictor is right more often); a branchless rewrite removes the branch so there is no k to pay at all. You measure first because on an already-predictable branch p is already tiny, so a branchless rewrite adds complexity for no gain — and may even be slower if it does more arithmetic unconditionally. Feed-forward: §2.4 warning box.
2.7 Step 4: The miss stalls the CPU only if there is no independent work to do while it is serviced. The deciding property is the amount of instruction-level parallelism in the surrounding code — whether there are nearby instructions whose inputs are ready and do not depend on the missing load. If there is enough such work, the out-of-order engine hides the miss latency behind it; if the code is a tight dependency chain that all waits on the loaded value, the machine has nothing else to do and stalls for the full miss. It is that property, not the miss latency alone, that decides the outcome, because the latency is a fixed cost of reaching DRAM — what varies, and what you control by how you write the code, is whether the CPU can overlap useful work with it. Feed-forward: §2.3 (out-of-order) and Chapter 1 §1.2 (miss latency).
2.8 (a) Branch prediction — sorting changed only predictability, not arithmetic. (b) Dependency chain / ILP — splitting an accumulator exposes independent work. (c) Memory hierarchy — a linked list scatters accesses to random addresses (cache misses, Chapter 1) where an array streams contiguously. (d) None of the three is a bottleneck — no branches, no memory pressure, presumably enough ILP — so the loop is already near peak; the lesson is that when none of the mechanisms is being violated, there is little constant-factor slack left to recover. Method-selection cue: match the symptom — "sorting helped" → branches; "extra accumulators helped" → ILP; "layout/pointers hurt" → memory.
2.9 The real cost model (Chapter 1 §1.4) resolves it: equal big-O guarantees equal scaling, never equal speed; a 5× gap lives entirely in the constant factor big-O discards. Three independent mechanisms that could each cause it: (1) memory access pattern — one version streams cache-friendly memory, the other chases pointers into DRAM (Chapter 1, Chapter 3); (2) branch misprediction — one has an unpredictable data-dependent branch flushing the pipeline (§2.4); (3) dependency chains / low ILP — one serializes its work and starves the superscalar units (§2.3). The single identifying action: profile / measure (e.g. with a profiler reporting cache misses and branch mispredictions) — the mechanism is an empirical question, not one big-O can answer. Tempting wrong answer: "it's impossible / the benchmark is wrong," which is the Chapter 1 trap of trusting big-O for a speed question. Feed-forward: §2.5 and Chapter 1 §1.4.
2.10 (a) On typical code branches are highly predictable, so speculation is almost always correct and the CPU keeps working instead of stalling several cycles at every branch — the occasional wasted work is far cheaper than stalling on every branch. (b) On an unpredictable branch the predictor is wrong a large fraction of the time, so much speculative work is discarded and the misprediction penalty dominates — a net loss versus not having to speculate at all. (c) At a high level: because speculatively executed instructions can affect microarchitectural state (such as what ends up in the cache) even when their results are later discarded, that residual state can, in principle, be observed and used to infer data that should not have been accessible — this is the basis of the real speculative-execution vulnerability class. The precise mechanisms and mitigations are a genuine, separate topic (touched on in Volume 4); describing them accurately requires primary sources, and this answer deliberately does not invent specifics. No-fabrication note: full credit requires the high-level reasoning and the acknowledgement that the details need real sources, not invented ones.
2.11 Machine- and compiler-specific by design. A correct write-up reports two measured times (single vs. four accumulators) and their ratio, with the four-accumulator version typically faster when the compiler has not already reassociated or vectorized the single-accumulator loop. It must state which numbers are the reader's own and note the ratio depends on CPU and compiler. Crucially, if optimization collapses the difference (the compiler reassociates or auto-vectorizes both), the correct response is to report that and describe what was observed — never to quote a ratio that was not actually measured. Method note: the exercise is as much about honest measurement discipline (no fabricated numbers) as about ILP. Feed-forward: §2.3 threeways box.

Chapter 3 — Solutions

3.1 64 / 8 = 8 doubles per line. Reading one from a cold line brings in the whole line, so the 7 neighbors become cheap hits. This rewards spatial locality — you get the nearby elements for free because memory arrives a full line at a time.
3.2 Temporal: a loop accumulator sum += x[i] — sum is reused every iteration, so after its first access it stays resident (retention of recently used lines). Spatial: walking x[0], x[1], x[2], … — consecutive elements share lines (line fill) and the sequential pattern lets the prefetcher fetch ahead. Line fill and prefetching exploit spatial locality; keeping recent lines exploits temporal.
3.3 (a) Compulsory (cold) — first-ever reference to those lines. (b) Capacity — the 4 GB working set vastly exceeds the 8 MB cache, so lines are evicted before reuse. (c) Conflict — a specific power-of-two row length aligns many accesses onto the same cache sets, so they evict each other despite free space elsewhere.
3.4 (a) Inner loop over columns (row-major order) is faster: consecutive accesses are adjacent in memory (stride 1), so each 64-byte line is fully used and the prefetcher runs ahead. Inner loop over rows strides by N elements, touching a new line almost every access. (b) Same big-O and same additions govern scaling, not speed; the constant factor — memory moved and misses incurred — differs by roughly an order of magnitude because only one version has spatial locality (this is the Chapter 1 §1.4 point, now concrete). (c) The slow version suffers mostly capacity misses (the whole matrix far exceeds cache, and its poor locality means it re-fetches lines it effectively wasted) — with a real conflict component too, since the power-of-two dimension (N = 8192) gives a power-of-two stride that aliases into a few cache sets (the very symptom §3.4 described); its lack of spatial reuse is what turns each fetch into wasted bandwidth. Tempting wrong answer: "they're both O(N2) so the difference must be a measurement error" — the §3.6 trap. Feed-forward: §3.6.
3.5 Replace the array-of-pointers with a contiguous array of the objects themselves (array of structs, or a struct-of-arrays if you only touch some fields), laid out in traversal order. Why it reduces misses: the objects now share cache lines, so walking them in order has spatial locality — each fetched line yields several objects instead of one random-heap object per pointer (fewer misses). Why it helps hide the rest: sequential, contiguous access is prefetchable and, unlike pointer-chasing, does not force a dependency chain where each object's address depends on reading the previous one — so the out-of-order engine (Chapter 2 §2.3) can overlap independent accesses and hide the misses that remain. Method note: the two wins are distinct — locality (fewer misses) and independence (hide the misses) — and the pointer layout loses on both. Feed-forward: §3.5.
3.6 (a) 8 bytes used of 64 fetched = 1/8 of each line. (b) A stride-1 traversal uses all 8 values per line, so the stride-8 traversal moves roughly 8× more memory for the same values. (c) That ~8× is a floor on the slowdown from wasted bandwidth alone; the measured row-major/column-major ratio was larger (~24–26×) because real effects compound it — two that push the measured number above the naive estimate: (i) the hardware prefetcher helps the sequential (row-major) loop even more, widening the gap; (ii) loss of memory-level parallelism / stalling on the strided loop, and possibly TLB misses from touching many pages, add cost the simple bytes-moved model ignores. No-fabrication note: the 8× is arithmetic; the ~25× is measured — do not present the estimate as the measurement. Feed-forward: §3.6.
3.7 Step 4: In this particular experiment the dominant lever is the number of misses (locality), not the inability to hide each one. The column-major loop touches a new line almost every iteration and uses only 1 of 8 values per line, so it issues roughly 8× as many line fetches and moves many times more memory than the row-major loop; that sheer volume of DRAM traffic is the main cost. The dependency argument is secondary here because both versions are simple predictable summations with similar per-iteration dependency structure — what differs overwhelmingly is how many expensive lines each one demands.
