A correct write-up: (a) computes fanout ≈ (page−header)/(key+pointer) and tabulates height across N, showing single-digit heights even at a trillion keys; (b) implements a working B-tree of some order m, inserts in a seeded order, reports measured height and split count, and checks height against the bracket ceil(log-base-m of N) ≤ height ≤ ceil(log-base-⌈m/2⌉ of N); (c) states toolchain and CPU and notes the fanout table is exact arithmetic and the tree height is a structural outcome of a deterministic insert order — neither is a wall-clock timing, so both are reproducible and hardware-independent. Tempting wrong answer: reporting the tree height as a performance measurement — it is a structural property, not a clock reading. Feed-forward: §51.3–§51.4.

Chapter 52 — Solutions

52.1 Borrowing moves one key from a sibling that has a spare, rotating it through the parent separator, and leaves the tree's structure unchanged; merging fuses the under-full node with a sibling into one node and pulls the parent's separator key down between them, destroying a node. Tempting wrong answer: “borrow moves a key directly between siblings” — it must pass through the parent, because the separator has to stay between the two children. Feed-forward: §52.1.
52.2 It shrinks at the root: when a merge propagates all the way up and empties the root, the root is removed and its single remaining child becomes the new root, dropping the height by one. Tempting wrong answer: “the tree shrinks by making a leaf shallower” — leaves never change depth individually; height changes only at the root, symmetric with growth. Feed-forward: §52.1.
52.3 About 69% full — the constant ln 2 ≈ 0.693 (Yao 1978, measured here at 0.684–0.687). An index built by insertion carries about 1/ln 2 ≈ 1.44× the pages of the same keys bulk-loaded — roughly 44% more. Tempting wrong answer: “about 100% full” — that is bulk-loading; naive 50/50 splits leave nodes averaging ln 2. Feed-forward: §52.3.
52.4 (a) A merge destroys a node (fusing two into one) and pulls a key down from the parent to sit between them — the exact reverse of a split, which creates a node and pushes a key up. (b) Pulling the separator down removes a key from the parent, which may itself drop below the minimum and merge, and so on up the tree. (c) The height decreases only when the merge reaches the root and leaves it with no keys and one child: that child becomes the new root. Because a whole level is removed uniformly at the top, every leaf loses the same one level, so all leaves stay at the same depth. Tempting wrong answer: “a merge anywhere lowers the height” — only a root-emptying merge does; internal merges just reduce a parent's key count. Feed-forward: §52.1.
52.5 (a) An eager merge locks three pages at once — the under-full node, its sibling, and the parent — and may propagate and lock more, which is heavy contention to spend on the common case where the slot is soon refilled; so engines defer it. (b) Index bloat is the index keeping its page count as live keys fall: occupancy drops toward the deleted fraction and range scans still walk the mostly-empty pages, paying fetches for absent keys. (c) A rebuild (REINDEX, or drop-and-recreate) reclaims the space; it is denser because it bulk-loads the surviving keys bottom-up, packing nodes to ~100% rather than leaving the under-full pages the deletes created. Tempting wrong answer: “lazy deletion is a bug” — it is a deliberate space-for-concurrency trade. Feed-forward: §52.2.
52.6 (a) About 69% (ln 2), implying a size ratio 1/ln 2 ≈ 1.44. (b) Roughly 1,440,000 pages — about 44% more than the 1,000,000 packed pages. (c) The extra pages cost more buffer-pool space (fewer of the index's pages stay resident, so more look-ups miss to disk) and, because lower occupancy means lower effective fanout, the tree can be a level taller, adding a page fetch to some look-ups. Tempting wrong answer: “the extra pages only waste disk” — they also cost cache residency and can add height. Feed-forward: §52.3.
52.7 (a) At most two at any moment — the current node and its parent — released as the search moves down; that is enough because crabbing never lets go of the parent until the child is safely latched, so no concurrent change can move a node out from under the descent. (b) It may hold the entire root-to-leaf path (up to the height) latched; it can release the ancestors only once it reaches a node that is safe — has room, so a change there cannot push a split upward. (c) When nodes are near-full, almost no node on the path is “safe,” so ancestor latches (including the root's) are held for the whole descent, and inserts serialize on the root. Tempting wrong answer: “a read also holds the whole path” — a read holds only one or two latches; it is the insert's split-safety that forces path-long holds. Feed-forward: §52.4.
52.8 Step 4: The search compares its target to the leaf's recorded high key, sees the target now exceeds it, and follows the right-link to the new sibling that the split created — where its key now lives — and continues there. Because any downward move a split makes can be recovered by moving right, the search never needed the parent latch to protect against a split below it; the right-link makes the split locally recoverable, so one latch at a time suffices. Tempting wrong answer: “it must restart from the root” — the right-link lets it move sideways to the sibling without re-descending. Feed-forward: §52.4.
52.9 (a) Lazy deletion — under-full pages are tolerated, not merged, so the page count holds. (b) Bulk-loading — the rebuild packs nodes to ~100% versus ln 2. (c) Borrow — a single key moved from a sibling, no structural change. (d) Merge — the only operation that can lower height, when it empties the root. (e) The right-link — the search follows it sideways after a concurrent split. Tempting wrong answer: attributing (b) to borrow or merge — density comes from bulk-loading the survivors, not from rebalancing. Feed-forward: §52.1–§52.4.
52.10 (a) True — height decreases only when a merge propagates to and empties the root. (b) False — random insertion averages ln 2 ≈ 69%, not 85%. (c) True — building bottom-up from sorted data fills each node and never splits, so it packs to ~100%. (d) False — deletion is usually lazy, leaving under-full pages; the index shrinks only on a rebuild. (e) False — the right-link's whole point is that a search holds only one latch and recovers a split by moving right, needing no parent latch. Tempting wrong answer: marking (d) true because “deletes free space” — they free logical entries, not on-disk pages, until a rebuild. Feed-forward: §52.1–§52.4.
52.11 (a) Insert: descend, and if the node is full, create a new node, move half the keys to it, push a separator up — propagating up, growing at the root. Delete: descend, and if the node underflows, merge with a sibling, move its keys in, pull a separator down — propagating up, shrinking at the root. Each step of one reverses a step of the other. (b) In practice the split is unavoidable (an over-full node cannot hold its keys) but an under-full node is still correct to read and search, so the merge can be safely skipped; deferring it avoids the three-page lock, breaking the symmetry for performance. (c) Insertion alone only reaches ln 2 occupancy, and deferred merges leave deleted pages under-full, so a long-lived tree drifts to ever-lower density; periodic rebuilds (or online reorganization) counter the drift by repacking. Tempting wrong answer: “the merge is skipped because it is incorrect” — it is correct but costly; it is skipped for concurrency, not correctness. Feed-forward: §52.1–§52.3.
52.12 Open-ended and platform-specific. A correct write-up: (a) implements a minimum-degree t B-tree with split on insert and borrow/merge on delete; (b) inserts a seeded random key order and reports average node occupancy converging on ln 2 ≈ 0.693 across a few t (this chapter measured 0.684–0.687 at t = 16, 32, 64); (c) deletes most keys and shows the height shrinking with all survivors still found; (d) states toolchain and notes occupancy and height are structural results of a deterministic operation sequence — reproducible and hardware-independent, not wall-clock timings. Tempting wrong answer: reporting occupancy or height as a performance number — both are structural properties of the tree's shape. Feed-forward: §52.3.

Chapter 53 — Solutions

53.1 The LSM-tree refuses to update pages in place; instead of finding a key's page and rewriting it (a random write), it buffers writes and flushes them sequentially. The Chapter 46 measurement that makes this pay is that sequential access (~916 MB/s) is about 49× faster than random 4 KiB access (~19 MB/s). Tempting wrong answer: “it avoids writing to disk” — it writes plenty, but only sequentially. Feed-forward: §53.1.
53.2 In order: the write-ahead log (WAL), then the memtable, then — when the memtable fills — the flushed SSTable. The WAL exists purely for durability: it is the sequential, fsync'd record that lets the in-memory memtable be rebuilt after a crash. Tempting wrong answer: naming the SSTable as the durability mechanism — the SSTable is the eventual sorted file; the WAL is what makes an in-RAM write survive a crash before the flush. Feed-forward: §53.2.
53.3 A delete writes a tombstone — a marker “this key is deleted” — into the memtable, which flushes like any other write. It cannot remove the key from disk because SSTables are immutable, so the old value still sits in older files; the tombstone, being newest, shadows it at read time. Tempting wrong answer: “it erases the key from the file” — immutability forbids that; deletion is by shadowing, not erasure. Feed-forward: §53.3.
53.4 (a) Appending in arrival order never seeks — every write is a pure sequential append, the fast side of the Chapter 46 gap. (b) A point read is catastrophic because the log is in arrival order, not key order, so the key could be anywhere and must be scanned for; and you cannot stop at the first match from the front, because a later append may hold a newer value, so the newest copy is whichever is last in the log. (c) Sortedness: keep the memtable sorted and flush it sorted, so each file is internally sorted — found by binary search in one file, and merged linearly across two like mergesort's merge step. Tempting wrong answer: “scan from the back and stop at the first match” — correct for finding the newest value but still a full-file scan per read; sortedness is what removes the scan. Feed-forward: §53.1–§53.2.
53.5 (a) The memtable, then the SSTables newest to oldest; newest must win because a later write shadows an earlier one, so the first source holding the key has its current value and older copies are superseded. (b) After put v2 (flush): read = v2. After put v3 (flush): read = v3 (the newer of two SSTables shadows v2). After delete (flush): read = None (the tombstone, newest, shadows v3 and v2, which still sit on disk). (c) A point miss must touch every source, because only after finding the key in none of them can it conclude absence — it can never stop early. Tempting wrong answer: “a hit is the worst case because it reads a value” — a hit can stop at the first source that has the key; a miss cannot stop at all. Feed-forward: §53.3.
53.6 (a) It keeps writes sequential (no file is ever randomly rewritten) and makes files safe to read concurrently and to cache, since nothing mutates under a reader. (b) An update just writes the new value into the memtable, which flushes to a newer SSTable; the newer copy shadows the old at read time. (c) Since the old value cannot be erased from its immutable file, deletion writes a tombstone that, being newest, shadows the old value instead. Tempting wrong answer: “immutability only helps concurrency” — its first purpose is keeping every write sequential. Feed-forward: §53.2–§53.3.
53.7 (a) The number of SSTables is the total writes divided by the flush threshold (roughly 100,000/1,000 ≈ 99 and 100,000/5,000 ≈ 19 in the model), since each threshold's worth of writes flushes one file. (b) A miss scans all of them (99, then 19); the miss is the worst case because it cannot stop at a first hit — the key is in none of the files, so every one must be probed. (c) A larger flush threshold means a larger memtable held in volatile RAM and more writes to replay from the WAL after a crash — more memory and slower recovery. Tempting wrong answer: “just make the threshold huge” — that trades read amplification for memory and crash-recovery time. Feed-forward: §53.3–§53.4.
53.8 Step 4: Each processed-and-deleted row left a tombstone, and every tombstone in the scanned range must be read and skipped, because each might be shadowing a live value in an older run — the scan cannot know without reading it. So a range that has churned through tens of thousands of insert/delete cycles holds tens of thousands of tombstones over its ~10 live rows, and the scan physically reads all of them to return almost nothing. It gets fast again only when a compaction merges the runs and drops the tombstones (and the values they shadow) from that range. Tempting wrong answer: “add an index on the range” — the cost is the tombstones themselves; only compaction removes them. Feed-forward: §53.3–§53.4.
53.9 (a) The WAL — a crash replays the log to rebuild the memtable, so no acknowledged write is lost. (b) Read amplification — a miss probes every file. (c) The tombstone — a deleted key's marker and its shadowed value occupy space until compaction. (d) The memtable — recent writes are served from RAM. (e) SSTable immutability — nothing mutates the file, so it needs no read lock. Tempting wrong answer: crediting (a) to the memtable — the memtable is volatile; it is the WAL that survives the crash. Feed-forward: §53.2–§53.4.
53.10 (a) False — even the flush is a sequential write; an LSM-tree issues no random writes. (b) False — a delete writes a tombstone and adds data; space is reclaimed only by compaction. (c) False — a read returns the value from the newest source that contains the key. (d) True — both the WAL append and the flush are sequential. (e) True — that is exactly read amplification. Tempting wrong answer: marking (a) true because “the flush goes to a specific place” — the flush is one large sequential write of a whole sorted file, not a random update. Feed-forward: §53.1–§53.4.
53.11 (a) Write cost: B-tree updates a leaf in place (random write, expensive) vs LSM appends sequentially (cheap). Read cost: B-tree descends one shallow tree (cheap) vs LSM merges many sorted runs (read amplification). Space: B-tree packs to ~69% and holds one copy vs LSM lets dead versions and tombstones linger until compaction (loose). (b) The LSM's write amplification comes from compaction re-reading and re-writing data that was already written; it is the counterpart to the B-tree's random-write cost, but it is deferred (paid later, in the background) and sequential (large merges), whereas the B-tree's is immediate and random (per insert). (c) B-tree is the right default for read- and range-scan-heavy workloads that update in place; the LSM-tree for write- and ingest-heavy workloads that can afford background merging and looser space. Tempting wrong answer: “the LSM has no write cost” — it defers the cost into compaction as write amplification. Feed-forward: §53.1–§53.5.
53.12 Open-ended and platform-specific. A correct write-up: (a) implements a sorted memtable that flushes to an immutable sorted SSTable at a threshold, a newest-to-oldest read, and a tombstone delete; (b) drives it with a seeded write stream over a small key space and reports the SSTable count (writes / threshold) and the files a point miss must scan; (c) verifies newest-write-wins and tombstone-shadows-value (this chapter's model: 99 and 19 SSTables at thresholds 1,000 and 5,000, a miss scanning all of them, get = v3 then None after the delete); (d) states toolchain and notes the file count and scan count are structural outcomes of the logic and the key stream — reproducible, not wall-clock timings. Tempting wrong answer: timing the reads and reporting milliseconds as the result — the reproducible quantities are the structural counts. Feed-forward: §53.3.

Chapter 54 — Solutions

54.1 It reclaims superseded update versions (keeping only the newest value per key) and deleted data; a tombstone it meets is dropped along with the older values it was shadowing, since after the merge no older run remains to hide them. Tempting wrong answer: “it keeps the tombstone forever” — the tombstone is dropped once compaction has merged past every value it shadowed. Feed-forward: §54.1.
54.2 Write amplification (compaction rewrites data as it merges into larger runs), read amplification (a lookup probes several runs), and space amplification (dead versions and tombstones linger until compaction removes them). Tempting wrong answer: naming only write and read — space amplification is the third and the one size-tiered blows up most. Feed-forward: §54.2.
54.3 Leveled compaction minimizes read (and space) amplification by keeping one run per level; size-tiered minimizes write amplification by writing each byte about once per level. Tempting wrong answer: “leveled minimizes write amplification” — it is the opposite; leveled pays the most in writes. Feed-forward: §54.3.
54.4 (a) The keyspace was small (5,000) and the runs overlapped, so most of the 25,934 entries were superseded updates or tombstones of the same keys; only the newest live value of each surviving key remained — 3,362 entries. (b) It became 1× for that range: the merged output is a single run, so a read touches one file instead of twenty. (c) Compaction still read all 25,934 inputs and wrote 3,362 outputs; that rewriting of already-stored data is write amplification, the cost paid to lower read and space amplification. Tempting wrong answer: “compaction is free because it shrinks the data” — it shrinks stored data but spends write bandwidth to do it. Feed-forward: §54.1–§54.2.
54.5 (a) The RUM conjecture: optimizing any two of read overhead, update overhead, and memory/space overhead comes at the expense of the third. (b) Aggressive compaction merges runs promptly, so few runs and little dead data (low read and space) but constant rewriting (high write); lazy compaction merges rarely, so little rewriting (low write) but many runs and much dead data (high read and space). (c) Both engines face read/update/space; the B-tree spends it as immediate random writes and tight space, the LSM-tree as deferred sequential write amplification and looser space — same trilemma, different corner. Tempting wrong answer: “the LSM-tree escapes the trade the B-tree faced” — it relocates the trade, it does not escape it. Feed-forward: §54.2.
54.6 (a) Leveled keeps exactly one sorted run per level; size-tiered lets up to T runs accumulate per level and merges them together when the level fills. (b) Leveled: promoting data into a level that is T× bigger rewrites ~T bytes per byte, across L levels → ~T×L; size-tiered: each byte is written once per level (in the bulk merge) → ~L. (c) Leveled: at most one run per level, so a read checks ~L runs; size-tiered: up to T runs per level, so a read checks ~T×L. Tempting wrong answer: assuming both read and write scale the same way — they scale oppositely, which is the whole trade. Feed-forward: §54.3.
54.7 (a) Leveled — read amplification 3 and space 1.10 keep latency low and waste little of the expensive storage, at the cost of write amplification 30, which a read-critical index can afford. (b) Size-tiered — write amplification 3 spares the cheap disk's write bandwidth and wear, and the firehose can tolerate read amplification 30 and 10× space on cheap storage. (c) About 30 TB hit the device (30×1 TB); it matters because an SSD's endurance is finite writes, so 30× amplification burns through its rated lifetime ~30× faster. Tempting wrong answer: “pick leveled everywhere because low read amp is always best” — for the firehose its 30× write amplification is the dominant cost. Feed-forward: §54.3–§54.4.
54.8 Step 4: This is a write stall (write throttling). It appears exactly at peak write load because that is when ingest most outruns compaction: the top-level runs pile up faster than they can be merged, read amplification there climbs, and the engine throttles writes to keep it bounded — so the “fast writes” degrade precisely when they are busiest. Two levers: provision more compaction throughput (I/O bandwidth and threads) so merging keeps pace, and/or move to a compaction family with lower write amplification (size-tiered) so less merging is needed per byte — accepting its higher read and space cost. Tempting wrong answer: “add more memory to the memtable” — a bigger memtable delays but does not remove the stall; the bottleneck is compaction throughput versus ingest. Feed-forward: §54.4.
54.9 (a) Write amplification — the device physically writes several times the logical volume. (b) Space amplification — dead versions and tombstones inflate on-disk size well past live data. (c) Read amplification — many runs probed per level. (d) Leveled compaction — one run per level. (e) Size-tiered compaction — merges a level's runs when it fills. Tempting wrong answer: crediting (a) to read amplification — reads do not wear the device; writes do. Feed-forward: §54.2–§54.3.
54.10 (a) False — the RUM tension means no strategy makes all three small; you spend one to save another. (b) False — compaction merges sorted runs in one sequential pass, reading and writing sequentially. (c) True — size-tiered trades higher read and space for lower write amplification. (d) False — compaction contends for device bandwidth and buffer pool and can cause write stalls, affecting foreground latency. (e) True — levels ≈ log-base-T, so larger T means fewer levels. Tempting wrong answer: marking (d) true because “background” sounds free — it is real work on the same device. Feed-forward: §54.1–§54.4.
54.11 (a) B-tree: low read, high (random) write, low space (~69% fill) — one point. Leveled-LSM: low read, high write, low space — but write is deferred and sequential. Size-tiered-LSM: high read, low write, high space. Each coordinate follows from the mechanism (in-place update; one-run-per-level; many-runs-per-level). (b) By varying T and choosing the compaction family, the LSM-tree reaches many points along the read/write/space surface, whereas the B-tree's in-place discipline fixes it near one; that tunability lets high-ingest systems place their cost where they can afford it. (c) The best point depends on the workload's read/write/space sensitivity, and the RUM conjecture says no point is best on all three — so the answer is a function of the workload, not of the engine. Tempting wrong answer: “the LSM-tree is strictly better because it's tunable” — tunable means it can be set badly too; it is better only when the workload wants a corner the B-tree can't reach. Feed-forward: §54.2–§54.5.
54.12 Open-ended and platform-specific. A correct write-up: (a) implements a k-way merge keeping the newest value per key and dropping tombstones, reporting input and output counts and the reclaimed fraction (this chapter: 25,934 → 3,362, 87% reclaimed); (b) computes write/read/space amplification for leveled (~T×L / ~L / ~1) and size-tiered (~L / ~T×L / ~T) across a few T; (c) states toolchain and notes the reclaimed fraction is a structural outcome of the merge logic and the amplification figures are exact model arithmetic — reproducible and hardware-independent, neither a wall-clock timing. Tempting wrong answer: reporting the amplification numbers as measured device throughput — they are a model of the structure, not a benchmark. Feed-forward: §54.3.
